First, existing detectors each rely on a single signal type — attention patterns (SinkProbe, AUROC 0.89 on HaluEval-QA), hidden-state dynamics (EigenTrack, 0.82–0.94 AUROC; HSAD via FFT), or log-probabilities (HALT via GRU) — with no principled way to combine them. This conflict persists because all comparisons are static — they collapse temporal dynamics into single snapshots, ignoring that different signals may carry complementary information at different generation stages. Second, and more critically, no existing method optimizes for early detection — identifying hallucination from partial responses (e.g., after only 25% of tokens are generated). Current detectors are trained and evaluated on complete responses, yet real-time guardrails must act as early as possible. Early time series classification is well-established in other domains (MultiETSC, RL-based early classifiers) but has never been applied to hallucination detection during LLM generation. These two gaps — no multi-signal temporal fusion, no early-detection optimization — mean practitioners building real-time hallucination guardrails must choose a single signal type with no principled basis, deploy a detector that cannot be trusted until generation is nearly complete, and sacrifice either accuracy (single signal) or latency (waiting for full response).\", \"opportunity\": \"Five independent research threads converge to make adaptive temporal fusion both possible and timely. (1) Signal validation: SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697) established attention sinks, EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735) validated hidden-state spectral features, and HALT (arXiv 2602.02888) proved log-probability time series — each independently effective for hallucination detection via temporal modeling, but never combined. The foundational basis for internal-state hallucination detection was established by INSIDE (ICLR 2024), which showed that LLMs' internal states retain hallucination-detection power via EigenScore, an eigenvalue-based metric on hidden-state covariance matrices. (2) Causal grounding: SinkTrack (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that modifying attention sinks causally affects hallucination; ReDeEP (ICLR 2025) showed Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads carry mechanistically distinct hallucination information — establishing that different signal types carry independent, non-redundant information. (3) Temporal complementarity evidence: Hallucination as Trajectory Commitment (arXiv 2604.15400) showed residual-stream trajectories bifurcate at the first generated token in 44.3% of prompts, while Shadows in the Attention (arXiv 2505.16894) found attention-locking thresholds emerge gradually — suggesting attention and hidden-state signals have fundamentally different temporal profiles, creating an opportunity for fusion. (4) Cross-modal fusion precedent: Attention-based fusion of multiple temporal signal streams is well-established in multivariate time series anomaly detection (MFGAN, DSAC) and multi-modal monitoring, but has never been applied to LLM internal signals. (5) Early classification methodology: Prefix-based multi-horizon training for time series is mature (tslearn, MultiETSC), providing the methodological foundation for optimizing detection at partial observation.\\n\\nThe key insight: if different signals carry complementary information at different generation stages (attention sinks as routing indicators, hidden states as computation indicators, log-probs as confidence indicators), then a learned time-varying fusion should outperform any fixed single-signal detector, and optimizing for early detection should yield faster-acting guardrails. We test this with TemporalFuse — the first adaptive multi-signal temporal fusion method for hallucination detection during autoregressive generation. The fusion architecture is the primary methodological contribution; the analysis of learned signal weights provides the first temporal comparison of signal types as an interpretable byproduct.\", \"approach\": \"We propose TemporalFuse, an adaptive temporal fusion method that learns time-varying weights over three internal signal streams — attention sinks, hidden-state spectral features, and log-probabilities — to detect hallucination during autoregressive generation, optimized for the earliest possible detection. The primary methodological contribution is the fusion architecture and early-detection training objective; the analysis of learned fusion weights provides the first temporal signal comparison as an interpretable byproduct.\\n\\n**Theoretical Motivation: Why Fusion Should Outperform Single Signals.** The three signal types occupy different positions in the transformer's computational pipeline: attention heads function as information routing (WHERE the model reads — Wu et al., ICLR 2025), hidden states represent accumulated computation (WHAT the model has computed — FFN key-value memories, Geva et al., EMNLP 2021), and log-probabilities reflect output confidence (HOW certain the model is). Because routing decisions causally precede the computation they gate, and both precede the output distribution, these signals should carry complementary information: a routing error may appear in attention features before the residual stream incorporates erroneous information, while confidence collapse in log-probs may be the most direct indicator of hallucination once it manifests. If the signals are temporally complementary (shifting at different times and rates), learned fusion can outperform any individual signal by attending to the most informative signal at each generation stage. If they are temporally redundant, fusion still cannot underperform the best individual signal (it can learn to assign all weight to one arm). This asymmetry makes fusion the principled default.\\n\\n**Architecture: Three-Arm Temporal Encoder + Cross-Signal Gating + Early-Detection Loss.**\\n\\nFor each generation, we extract three parallel feature streams at every decoding step t:\\n\\n*Arm 1 — SinkWatch (Attention Sinks):* Per-step features from top-K informative head-layer combinations (K=5–15) identified via SinkProbe's ℓ₁-regularized analysis: sink scores for top-k sink tokens (k=2–3), sink concentration, sink entropy, context-attention ratio, plus first-order temporal derivatives. Raw dim ~50–120.\\n\\n*Arm 2 — SpectralTrack (Hidden States):* Per-step spectral features from sliding-window covariance matrices of hidden-state activations: leading eigenvalues, spectral gaps, entropy, RMT statistics. Raw dim ~10–20.\\n\\n*Arm 3 — LogProbTrack (Log-Probabilities):* Per-step log-probability features: token log-prob, predictive entropy, top-k probability gap, rank. Matching HALT's design. Raw dim ~25.\\n\\nEach arm includes a per-arm learned linear projection to common dimension d=32, then feeds into an identical unidirectional GRU (hidden_dim=64, ~25K recurrent parameters). This adapts early time series classification methodology (MultiETSC, RL-based early classifiers) to hallucination detection for the first time, explicitly training the model to produce informative predictions before generation is complete. The loss encourages the gating network to attend to whichever signal carries the earliest discriminative information.\\n\\n**Primary Analyses (EMNLP Short Paper).** (1) Fusion vs. individual arms: AUROC/AUPRC comparing TemporalFuse against each individual arm, testing whether fusion outperforms the best single signal. (2) Early-detection curves: AUROC at observation fractions {0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0} for TemporalFuse vs. individual arms, demonstrating the benefit of multi-horizon training. (3) Temporal signal importance map: mean gate weights α_t across steps for factual vs. hallucinated generations — the first visualization of how optimal signal reliance changes during hallucination onset. (4) Static-vs-temporal ranking: comparing signal rankings from our learned gate weights against HALUPROBE's and Proxy Analyzers' static findings. Extract hidden states at each claim's token span across multiple layers (following Han et al.'s layer-group methodology). Train lightweight linear probes (logistic regression on span-aggregated hidden states) to predict continuous factuality confidence scores. Unlike Han et al.'s binary factuality labels, we train on soft labels derived from verification confidence, enabling graded uncertainty estimation.\\n\\n**Offline Stage 2 — Verbalized-Confidence Direction Extraction (included in Stage 1 compute; one-time per model):** Extract a verbalized-confidence steering direction via contrastive activation pairs: generate matched claim pairs where the same factual content is expressed with high confidence ('X was born in Y') vs. hedged uncertainty ('X was reportedly born in Y, though I am not certain'). The mean activation difference yields the steering direction, following the contrastive methodology from Ji et al. (VUF) and Miao & Ungar (CAA). For the 70B model, if the pilot reveals partial orthogonality degradation, we apply Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to project the confidence direction away from the accuracy direction before use.\\n\\n**Online Stage — Sub-Sentence Probe-Guided Steering During Generation:** During autoregressive generation: (1) At each generated token, run the factuality probe on its hidden states — this is a single matrix-vector multiplication with negligible overhead (~0.001% of the forward pass). (2) Maintain a running exponential moving average (EMA) of probe scores over a sliding window of the last K tokens (default K=8), providing smoothed uncertainty estimates that avoid triggering on single noisy tokens while enabling sub-sentence response. (3) When the EMA drops below the calibrated threshold θ, immediately activate steering — even mid-sentence. This means RaS can begin hedging within the current claim by steering subsequent tokens toward uncertainty-expressing language (e.g., generating qualifiers like 'reportedly,' 'I believe,' or reformulations for the remaining tokens in the sentence). ## SinkTrack Overview

SinkTrack mitigates two long-standing issues (hallucination and context forgetting) in decoder-only LLMs by exploiting the synergistic relationship between attention drift and attention sink.

## The Problem It Addresses

Attention sink is the tendency to consistently allocate high attention to the very first token (i.e., ⟨BOS⟩) of a sequence. SinkTrack treats ⟨BOS⟩ as an information anchor and injects key contextual features (such as those derived from the input image or instruction) into its representation.

## Overview

EigenTrack is an interpretable real-time detector that uses the spectral geometry of hidden activations, a compact global signature of model dynamics. Large language models (LLMs) offer broad utility but remain prone to hallucination and out-of-distribution (OOD) errors.

## Methodology

EigenTrack constructs sliding-window activation matrices, extracts covariance spectrum statistics including leading eigenvalues, spectral gaps, entropy, and Random Matrix Theory features based on divergence from the Marchenko-Pastur law, and streams these signals into a lightweight recurrent classifier to model temporal evolution.

This design detects shifts toward noise-like representation regimes, enabling early identification of hallucination and OOD behavior before surface-level errors appear.

## Key Advantages

Unlike black-box and grey-box methods that require multiple generations or log-probability access, EigenTrack operates with a single forward pass and no resampling. Unlike existing white-box detectors, it preserves temporal context, aggregates global signals, and offers interpretable accuracy-latency trade-offs.

## Performance

EigenTrack achieves AUROC values of 0.82 to 0.94 for hallucination detection and 0.85 to 0.96 for OOD detection across LLMs and VLMs. On LLaMa-7B, it reaches 0.89 AUROC for hallucination and 0.92 for OOD, outperforming baselines such as HaloScope, LapEigvals, and SelfCheckGPT while using only a lightweight recurrent head.

The paper was submitted on September 19, 2025, with the latest version (v4) released on February 6, 2026.

## Overview
HaluProbe is a framework that systematically extracts the internal states from large language model inference and provides a deep understanding of the generation of hallucinations.

## Key Contributions
The framework divides LLMs' inference process into three stages: understanding, query, and generation, and extracts 8 features from these three stages.

## Internal States and Features
HaluProbe extracts three types of internal state from the three stages during inference: Attention, which is the internal state in which LLMs understand the input context, extracting each attention score matrix from each transformer layer's head for each token. Additionally, the query stage involves layer representation, and the query stage involves processing contextual representations through a feedforward network to derive higher-level abstractions.

**Paper Details:**
- **arXiv ID:** 2505.16894

**Overview:**

This paper presents the first systematic study linking hallucination incidence to internal-state drift induced by incremental context injection in large language models.

**Methodology:**

The researchers construct two 16-round "titration" tracks per question: one appends relevant but partially flawed snippets, the other injects deliberately misleading content. Across six open-source LLMs, they track overt hallucination rates with a tri-perspective detector and covert dynamics via cosine, entropy, JS and Spearman drifts of hidden states and attention maps.
